title: Python Data Structures: Lists, Dicts, Sets & Collections
sub: Store, group, count and sort data with the right container, then summarize a web log in a few lines
goals: Choose between list, tuple, dict, set and frozenset by asking about order, mutability and lookup
Slice, unpack and copy sequences without tripping over aliasing
Write list, dict, set and generator comprehensions and read nested ones
Sort by one or several keys with sorted(), key= and a stable sort
Count, group and rank data with Counter, defaultdict, deque and namedtuple
Build the core of loganalyzer.py: parse log lines into records and summarize them

blocks.text: Programs are mostly data moving between containers: a list of log lines becomes a dict of counts, which becomes a ranked list, which becomes a report. Picking the right container decides whether the code is three lines or thirty, and whether it is fast or crawls on a million records. In this chapter you will learn the five built-in containers, the comprehension syntax that builds them, the sorting tools, and the `collections` module that adds counting and grouping. The examples are all network data: requests per IP, ports per host, ping times, two inventories to merge. You finish by writing the analysis core of `loganalyzer.py`.

Every `run` block can be edited. Before you run one, write the output you expect on paper. A wrong prediction is the quickest way to find a gap in your model. Open the playground and keep it beside the page.
Choosing a container
Ask three questions: does order matter, does the data change, and how will I look things up?

blocks.text: "Fast" means constant time on average: a dict or set with ten million entries answers `key in d` in about the same time as one with ten. A list must scan, so `x in big_list` takes time proportional to its length. That single fact turns many slow programs into fast ones: when you test membership repeatedly, put the data in a set or dict first.

blocks.code:
list  ┌───┬───┬───┬───┐     dict (hash table)         set
         │ a │ b │ c │ d │     key ──hash──▶ slot ──▶ value    key ──hash──▶ slot
         └───┴───┴───┴───┘     "10.0.0.1" ──▶ ●──▶ 142         "10.0.0.1" ──▶ ●
          0   1   2   3        jump straight to the slot        same table, no values
          x in list: walk       x in dict / set: compute the hash, look in one place

blocks.text: A **hash table** stores each key at a position computed from the key's **hash**, a number derived from its contents. That is why dict keys and set members must be **hashable**, which in practice means immutable: strings, numbers, tuples of those, `frozenset`. A list cannot be a key because changing it would change its hash and strand the entry.

blocks.text: Sequences: indexing, slicing, unpacking
Lists, tuples, strings and `range` objects share one interface: they are **sequences**. Everything in this section works on all of them.

blocks.code:
hops = ["gw", "isp", "core1", "core2", "edge", "server"]
print(hops[0], hops[-1], hops[-2])        # negative indexes count from the end
print(hops[1:4], hops[:2], hops[4:])      # [start:stop], stop excluded
print(hops[::2], hops[::-1])              # step; -1 reverses
print(hops[10:], len(hops[2:2]))          # out-of-range slices are empty, never errors
word = "handshake"
print(word[:4], word[-5:], word[::-1])    # strings are sequences of characters

blocks.text: A slice always returns a **new** object of the same type, and `seq[a:b]` has `b - a` items. Because the stop index is excluded, `seq[:n] + seq[n:]` is always the whole sequence. Indexing a single position that does not exist, on the other hand, raises `IndexError`.

tokens.exp: stop: first index NOT included (default len)
second separator, only needed to give a step
step: take every 2nd item; negative walks backwards

blocks.text: Tuples and unpacking
A tuple is an immutable list. Its real strength is **unpacking**: assigning the parts of a sequence to names in one statement.

blocks.code:
conn = ("192.168.1.23", 51514, "93.184.216.34", 443)
src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port = conn
print(dst_ip, dst_port)

first, *middle, last = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]     # * collects the rest into a list
print(first, middle, last)

head, *rest = "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1".split()
print(head, rest)

a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a                                # swap without a temp variable
print(a, b)

for ip, port in [("10.0.0.1", 22), ("10.0.0.2", 80)]:   # unpack in a for header
    print(f"{ip}:{port}")
single = (5,)
print(type(single), type((5)))              # the comma makes the tuple

blocks.text: The number of names on the left must match the number of items (or use one starred name to absorb the difference), otherwise Python raises `ValueError`. Unpacking is why functions can "return several values": they return a tuple and the caller unpacks it.

blocks.title: Tuples are immutable, their contents may not be

blocks.text: `t = ([1], [2])` cannot have its slots replaced, but `t[0].append(9)` works because the list inside is mutable. Immutability is shallow.
Lists in depth
A **list** is a resizable array of references. Most of its methods change it in place and return `None`, a design choice that catches beginners: `data = data.sort()` leaves `data` as `None`.

blocks.code:
samples = [11.8, 12.3, 14.9]
samples.append(13.0)
samples.extend([12.1, 11.9])
samples.insert(0, 20.5)
print(samples, len(samples))
print(samples.pop(), samples.pop(0), samples)
print(sorted(samples), samples)         # sorted() returns a new list; the original is unchanged
samples += [1.0, 2.0]                   # += extends in place
print(min(samples), max(samples), sum(samples) / len(samples))
print(12.3 in samples, 99 in samples)

blocks.text: Cost model, worth remembering: `append`/`pop()` at the end are cheap; `insert(0, x)`, `pop(0)` and `x in lst` are linear. If you need a queue (add at one end, remove at the other), use `collections.deque`, covered below.

blocks.name: list.append()
blocks.sum: Add one item to the end of a list, in place.

how.text: Mutates the list and returns `None`, so `lst = lst.append(x)` destroys your list. Adding one item at a time is cheap (amortized constant time).

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:
ports = [22, 80]
ports.append(443)
print(ports, ports.append(8080))

examples.desc: Collect the status codes from the log into a list
examples.code: awk '{print $9}' access.log | python3 -c 'import sys; codes = []; [codes.append(int(w)) for w in sys.stdin.read().split()]; print(len(codes), max(codes))'

gotchas: `append([1, 2])` adds the list as a single item. Use `extend` to add its elements.

blocks.name: list.extend()
blocks.sum: Append every item of an iterable to the end of a list.

how.text: Same effect as a loop of `append`, but faster. `lst += other` does the same in place.

examples.desc: Example

hosts.extend(['nas', 'pi'])
hosts.extend('ab')
print(hosts)

blocks.name: list.insert()
blocks.sum: Insert an item before a given index.

how.text: Shifts every later item one place right, so it is linear in the length of the list. Inserting at index 0 of a big list in a loop is slow; use `collections.deque` for that job.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:
q = ['b', 'c']
q.insert(0, 'a')
q.insert(99, 'z')
print(q)

examples.desc: Put a new first item in front of the lines on stdin
examples.code: printf 'b\nc\n' | python3 -c 'import sys; q = sys.stdin.read().split(); q.insert(0, "a"); print(q)'

gotchas: An index past the end simply appends; it does not raise an error.

blocks.name: list.remove()
blocks.sum: Delete the first item equal to a value.

how.text: Searches from the left and removes only the first match. Raises `ValueError` when the value is absent, so check with `in` first or catch the error.

examples.desc: Example
Drop the first occurrence of an address from a piped list
examples.code:
printf '10.0.0.1
10.0.0.2
10.0.0.1
' | python3 -c 'import sys; ips = sys.stdin.read().split(); ips.remove("10.0.0.1"); print(ips)'

gotchas: Removing items while looping over the same list skips elements. Loop over a copy (`for x in lst[:]`) or build a new list with a comprehension.

blocks.name: list.pop()
blocks.sum: Remove and return the item at an index (the last by default).

how.text: Popping the end is constant time; popping from the front shifts everything and is linear. Raises `IndexError` on an empty list.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:
stack = [1, 2, 3]
print(stack.pop(), stack.pop(0), stack)

examples.desc: Pop the last and first lines of a piped sequence
examples.code: seq 1 5 | python3 -c 'import sys; s = sys.stdin.read().split(); print(s.pop(), s.pop(0), s)'

blocks.name: list.clear()
blocks.sum: Remove every item, keeping the same list object.

how.text: Empties the list in place, so every other name bound to the same list sees it empty. `lst = []` instead rebinds only your name to a new list.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
a.clear()
print(a, b)

blocks.name: list.index()
blocks.sum: Return the position of the first item equal to a value.

how.text: Scans from the left. Raises `ValueError` if the value is absent. Optional `start` and `stop` limit the search range.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:

print(hops.index('isp'), hops.index('isp', 2))

isp
core
' | python3 -c 'import sys; hops = sys.stdin.read().split(); print(hops.index("core"))'

blocks.name: list.count()
blocks.sum: Count how many items equal a value.

how.text: A full scan each call. To count every distinct value at once, use `collections.Counter`.

examples.desc: Example

blocks.name: list.sort()
blocks.sum: Sort a list in place.

how.text: Returns `None` and reorders the list itself. The sort is stable. `key` takes one argument and returns the value to compare. Use `sorted()` when you need a new list and want to keep the original.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:
sizes = [1500, 64, 576]
sizes.sort(reverse=True)
names = ['Pi', 'nas', 'Gw']
names.sort(key=str.lower)
print(sizes, names)

examples.desc: Sort numbers read from a pipe
examples.code: seq 5 -1 1 | python3 -c 'import sys; n = [int(x) for x in sys.stdin.read().split()]; n.sort(); print(n)'

blocks.name: list.reverse()
blocks.sum: Reverse a list in place.

how.text: Swaps items end for end and returns `None`. `reversed(lst)` gives an iterator and `lst[::-1]` a reversed copy.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:
path = ['a', 'b', 'c']
path.reverse()
print(path, path[::-1])

examples.desc: Reverse the lines of a stream, like tac
examples.code: seq 1 4 | python3 -c 'import sys; a = sys.stdin.read().split(); a.reverse(); print(*a, sep="\n")'

blocks.name: list.copy()
blocks.sum: Return a shallow copy of a list.

how.text: Equivalent to `lst[:]` or `list(lst)`. The new list is a different object, but it holds the same item objects, so nested lists are shared. Use `copy.deepcopy` for a fully independent copy.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:
a = [[1], [2]]
b = a.copy()
b.append([3])
b[0].append(99)
print(a, b)

examples.desc: Copy a piped list, change the copy and compare
examples.code: seq 1 3 | python3 -c 'import sys; a = sys.stdin.read().split(); b = a.copy(); b.append("x"); print(a, b)'

gotchas: Shallow means one level deep: the inner lists are still shared.

blocks.text: Aliasing: two names, one list

Assignment never copies. `b = a` makes a second **name** for the same object, and a change through either name is visible through both. This is the most common source of "my data changed and I did not touch it" bugs.

blocks.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a                  # alias
c = a.copy()           # shallow copy
b.append(4)
print(a, b, c, a is b, a is c)

def add_hop(path, hop):
    path.append(hop)   # mutates the caller's list!
    return path

route = ["gw"]
add_hop(route, "isp")
print(route)

def add_hop_safe(path, hop):
    return path + [hop]  # builds a new list

print(add_hop_safe(route, "core"), route)

blocks.text: Shallow and deep copies

`copy()`, `list(a)` and `a[:]` make a **shallow copy**: a new outer list whose slots point at the same inner objects. For flat data of numbers and strings that is enough. For nested data you need `copy.deepcopy`.

blocks.code:
import copy
inventory = [{"host": "gw", "ports": [22]}, {"host": "nas", "ports": [80]}]
shallow = inventory.copy()
deep = copy.deepcopy(inventory)
inventory[0]["ports"].append(443)
print(shallow[0]["ports"], deep[0]["ports"])

grid_bad = [[0] * 3] * 3      # three references to ONE row
grid_bad[0][0] = 1
print(grid_bad)
grid_ok = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]   # a new row each time
grid_ok[0][0] = 1
print(grid_ok)

blocks.text: The `[[0] * 3] * 3` trap is the same aliasing in disguise: `*` repeats the reference, not the row. Build nested lists with a comprehension so each row is created separately.
`def f(items=[])` creates the list once, at definition time, and shares it across all calls (see [Python flow](#py-flow)). The idiom is `def f(items=None): items = [] if items is None else items`.

blocks.name: copy.deepcopy()
blocks.sum: Recursively copy an object and everything inside it.

how.text: Walks nested lists, dicts and sets and copies each one, so the result shares no mutable object with the original. It is slower than a shallow copy and follows reference cycles correctly.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:
import copy
a = {'ports': [22, 80]}
b = copy.deepcopy(a)
b['ports'].append(443)
print(a, b)

examples.desc: Deep-copy a record built from stdin, then change only the copy
examples.code: echo 22 80 | python3 -c 'import sys, copy; a = {"ports": sys.stdin.read().split()}; b = copy.deepcopy(a); b["ports"].append("443"); print(a, b)'

blocks.text: Dictionaries
A **dict** maps unique keys to values. It is the most useful structure in Python: JSON objects, records, counters, indexes and caches are all dicts. Since Python 3.7 a dict remembers insertion order.

blocks.code:
host = {"name": "gw", "ip": "192.168.1.1", "ports": [53, 80]}
print(host["name"], host.get("mac"), host.get("mac", "unknown"))
host["mac"] = "aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff"        # add
host["ip"] = "192.168.1.254"             # replace
del host["ports"]                        # remove
print(host, len(host))
print("ip" in host, "ports" in host)     # membership tests the KEYS

for key in host:                         # iterating gives keys
    print(key, "->", host[key])
for key, value in host.items():          # items() gives pairs
    print(f"{key:>5} = {value}")

try:
    host["vendor"]
except KeyError as err:
    print("KeyError:", err)

blocks.text: `d[key]` raises `KeyError` for a missing key; `d.get(key, default)` returns the default instead. Choose deliberately: use `[]` when a missing key is a bug you want to hear about, and `.get` when absence is normal.

tokens.exp: a dict that maps each item to how many times it was seen
the key: whatever you are counting
the current total, or 0 the first time we see this key

blocks.text: That loop is the pattern behind every frequency table. `collections.Counter` packages it, as you will see shortly.

blocks.name: dict.get()
blocks.sum: Return a value for a key, or a default when the key is missing.

how.text: Never raises `KeyError`. It does not insert the default, which makes it ideal for reading optional fields.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:
host = {'ip': '192.168.1.1'}
print(host.get('ip'), host.get('mac'), host.get('mac', 'unknown'))

blocks.name: dict.setdefault()
blocks.sum: Return the value for a key, inserting a default first if the key is missing.

how.text: One call that does "get, and if absent create". It is the classic way to group items into lists without `defaultdict`.

examples.desc: Example
Group ports per host from host/port lines
examples.code:
printf 'gw 53
nas 22
gw 80
' | python3 -c 'import sys; d = {}; [d.setdefault(h, []).append(p) for h, p in (l.split() for l in sys.stdin)]; print(d)'

gotchas: The default is built every time you call it, even if the key exists. For an expensive default use `defaultdict` or an `if key not in` test.

blocks.name: dict.update()
blocks.sum: Merge another mapping or key-value pairs into a dict, in place.

how.text: Existing keys are overwritten by the new values; new keys are added. `a | b` builds a new merged dict (Python 3.9 and later) and `a |= b` is the in-place form.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:
base = {'port': 80, 'tls': False}
base.update({'tls': True}, timeout=5)
print(base)
print({'a': 1} | {'a': 2, 'b': 3})

examples.code: python3 -c 'a = {"x": 1}; a.update({"y": 2}); print(a)'

blocks.name: dict.pop()
blocks.sum: Remove a key and return its value.

how.text: Without a default, a missing key raises `KeyError`; with one, you get the default back. Use it to take a field out of a record.

blocks.sum: Remove and return the last inserted key-value pair.

how.text: Since Python 3.7 it removes in last-in, first-out order, which makes a dict usable as a simple stack of pairs. Raises `KeyError` when empty.

blocks.name: dict.keys()
blocks.sum: Return a live view of the keys.

how.text: A view reflects later changes to the dict and supports set operations (`&`, `|`, `-`), which is a neat way to compare two inventories. `for k in d` already iterates the keys.

examples.desc: Example
List the distinct client IPs as sorted dict keys
examples.code: awk '{print $1, $9}' access.log | python3 -c 'import sys; d = dict(l.split() for l in sys.stdin); print(sorted(d.keys()))'

blocks.name: dict.values()
blocks.sum: Return a live view of the values.

how.text: Order matches insertion order. Values can repeat, so a values view does not support set operations. Convert with `list(d.values())` to index it.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:

print(sum(bytes_per_ip.values()), max(bytes_per_ip.values()))

blocks.name: dict.items()
blocks.sum: Return a live view of (key, value) pairs.

how.text: The standard way to loop over both parts. Combine with `sorted(..., key=...)` to rank by value, or unpack straight into names in a `for` header.

examples.desc: Example
Rank hosts by name length from a file

gotchas: Changing the dict's size while iterating a view raises `RuntimeError`. Iterate over `list(d.items())` if you must delete.

blocks.name: dict.fromkeys()
blocks.sum: Build a dict from keys that all share one starting value.

how.text: A class method. Every key gets the **same** value object, so never pass a mutable one like `[]`. With the default `None` it is a neat way to remove duplicates while keeping order.

blocks.sum: Remove every key from a dict, in place.

blocks.text: Dicts of lists and dicts of dicts

Real data nests. A dict of lists groups items under a key; a dict of dicts is an indexed table. This shape is exactly what `json.loads` returns, so everything here applies to API responses and config files.
Sets

A **set** is an unordered collection of unique, hashable items with fast membership tests and the algebra you remember from school. Network work uses it constantly: which hosts are new since yesterday, which ports are open on both machines, which addresses are in the allow-list.

blocks.code:
seen = set()
for ip in ["10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2", "10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.3", "10.0.0.2"]:
    seen.add(ip)
print(sorted(seen), len(seen))
print(len({"a", "b", "a"}), {1, 2} == {2, 1})

monday = {"10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2", "10.0.0.3"}
tuesday = {"10.0.0.2", "10.0.0.3", "10.0.0.9"}
print("both:    ", sorted(monday & tuesday))
print("either:  ", sorted(monday | tuesday))
print("new:     ", sorted(tuesday - monday))
print("gone:    ", sorted(monday - tuesday))
print("changed: ", sorted(monday ^ tuesday))
print(monday <= (monday | tuesday), {1}.isdisjoint({2}))

monday ─┐          ┌─ tuesday
       ┌───┴───┬──────┴───┐
       │ .1    │ .2  .3   │ .9
       │ only  │  both    │ only
       │ monday│          │ tuesday
       └───────┴──────────┘
   monday - tuesday = {.1}    monday & tuesday = {.2, .3}    monday ^ tuesday = {.1, .9}

blocks.text: Two practical notes. A set has no order, so `sorted(s)` before printing makes output reproducible. And removing duplicates with `list(set(items))` loses the original order; to keep first-seen order use `list(dict.fromkeys(items))`.

blocks.name: set.add()
blocks.sum: Add one element to a set.

how.text: Does nothing if the element is already present. Elements must be hashable: strings, numbers and tuples work; lists and dicts do not.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:
seen = {'10.0.0.1'}
seen.add('10.0.0.2')
seen.add('10.0.0.1')
print(sorted(seen))

blocks.name: set.remove()
blocks.sum: Remove an element; raise an error if it is missing.

how.text: Raises `KeyError` for an absent element, which is useful when absence would be a bug. Use `discard` when absence is fine.

Remove one value from a set built from stdin

blocks.name: set.discard()
blocks.sum: Remove an element if it is present; do nothing otherwise.

how.text: The forgiving version of `remove`. Never raises.

examples.desc: Example

s = {1, 2, 3}
s.discard(2)
s.discard(99)
print(s)

examples.desc: Discard a value that may not be in the piped data

blocks.name: set.union()
blocks.sum: Return a new set with the elements of all the sets.

how.text: Same as the `|` operator, but the method accepts any iterable, not only sets.

examples.desc: Example
Merge piped ports with a fixed list
examples.code: printf '22\n80\n' | python3 -c 'import sys; print(sorted(set(sys.stdin.read().split()) | {"80", "443"}))'

blocks.name: set.intersection()
blocks.sum: Return a new set of elements found in all the sets.

how.text: Same as `&`. Answers "which items are in both lists".

examples.desc: Example
Which of these addresses appear in ips.txt
examples.code: python3 -c 'a = set(open("ips.txt").read().split()); b = {"192.168.1.1", "10.0.0.5", "8.8.8.8"}; print(sorted(a & b))'

blocks.name: set.difference()
blocks.sum: Return a new set of elements in this set but not in the others.

how.text: Same as `-`. Order matters: `a - b` and `b - a` differ.

examples.desc: Example
Show log clients that are not on a known-hosts list
examples.code: awk '{print $1}' access.log | python3 -c 'import sys; known = {"10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.5"}; print(sorted(set(sys.stdin.read().split()) - known))'

blocks.name: set.symmetric_difference()
blocks.sum: Return the elements that are in exactly one of two sets.

how.text: Same as `^`. Equal to the union minus the intersection: everything that changed between two snapshots.

examples.desc: Example
What changed between a piped snapshot and a second one
examples.code: seq 1 3 | python3 -c 'import sys; print(sorted(set(sys.stdin.read().split()) ^ {"3", "4"}))'

blocks.name: set.issubset()
blocks.sum: Test whether every element of this set is in another.

how.text: Same as `<=`; `<` tests for a proper subset. The empty set is a subset of every set.

examples.desc: Example
Are all piped ports in the allowed set

blocks.name: set.issuperset()
blocks.sum: Test whether this set contains every element of another.

how.text: Same as `>=`. Reads naturally as "does the scan cover everything on the checklist".

examples.desc: Example
Does the piped scan cover the whole checklist
examples.code:

80
443
' | python3 -c 'import sys; print(set(sys.stdin.read().split()).issuperset({"22", "443"}))'

blocks.name: set.isdisjoint()
blocks.sum: Test whether two sets share no elements.

how.text: True when the intersection is empty. Faster than building the intersection and testing it.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code: print({22, 80}.isdisjoint({443, 8080}), {22, 80}.isdisjoint({80}))

examples.desc: Check that a piped list shares nothing with a blocklist

blocks.name: set.update()
blocks.sum: Add all elements of one or more iterables to a set, in place.

how.text: The in-place counterpart of `union`; also written `|=`. Accepts lists, tuples, strings and other sets.

examples.desc: Example
Pour piped lines into an existing set
examples.code: seq 1 3 | python3 -c 'import sys; s = {"9"}; s.update(sys.stdin.read().split()); print(sorted(s))'

blocks.sum: Remove and return an arbitrary element.

how.text: Sets have no order, so which element comes out is not defined. Raises `KeyError` on an empty set.

blocks.sum: Remove every element from a set.

how.text: In place, like the other `clear` methods.

blocks.name: set.copy()
blocks.sum: Return a shallow copy of a set.

how.text: Equivalent to `set(s)`. Set elements are immutable, so a shallow copy is all you ever need.

blocks.text: Constructors and conversions

The type names double as constructors that convert between containers. A conversion is how you change the properties of your data on purpose: `set()` to drop duplicates, `tuple()` to freeze a record, `list()` to materialize a lazy value, `dict(zip(...))` to pair two lists.

blocks.name: list()
blocks.sum: Build a list from any iterable, or an empty list.

how.text: Consumes the iterable once and stores the items. Use it to turn a `range`, a string, a dict's keys or a generator into a list you can index and change.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code: print(list('SYN'), list(range(3)), list({'a': 1, 'b': 2}), list())

examples.desc: Read stdin lines into a list and show the last two
examples.code: seq 1 5 | python3 -c 'import sys; print(list(sys.stdin)[-2:])'

blocks.name: tuple()
blocks.sum: Build a tuple from any iterable, or an empty tuple.

how.text: A tuple is an immutable sequence. Use it for fixed records such as `(ip, port)` pairs; because it is immutable and hashable (when its items are), it can be a dict key or a set element. A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: `(5,)`.

examples.desc: Example
Unique (client, status) pairs from the log as tuples
examples.code: awk '{print $1, $9}' access.log | python3 -c 'import sys; print(sorted({tuple(l.split()) for l in sys.stdin}))'

blocks.name: dict()
blocks.sum: Build a dict from pairs, keyword arguments or another mapping.

how.text: `dict([(k, v), ...])` and `dict(zip(keys, values))` are the usual ways to build a dict from parallel data. Keyword form only works for keys that are valid identifiers.

examples.desc: Example
Build a dict from piped name/value lines
examples.code: printf 'ip 10.0.0.1\nport 22\n' | python3 -c 'import sys; print(dict(l.split() for l in sys.stdin))'

blocks.name: set()
blocks.sum: Build a set from an iterable, or an empty set.

how.text: Drops duplicates and loses order. `{}` is an empty **dict**, so write `set()` for an empty set. Membership tests are constant time on average, which makes sets the right tool for "have I seen this".

examples.desc: Example
examples.code: print(sorted(set('mississippi')), type({}), type(set()), 3 in {1, 2, 3})

examples.desc: Count distinct client IPs, like sort -u | wc -l
examples.code: awk '{print $1}' access.log | python3 -c 'import sys; print(len(set(sys.stdin.read().split())))'

blocks.name: frozenset()
blocks.sum: Build an immutable, hashable set.

how.text: Supports all read-only set operations but no `add` or `remove`. Because it is hashable it can be a dict key or an element of another set, for example a set of port groups.

examples.desc: Example
Count distinct port groups regardless of order
examples.code:
printf '22 80
80 22
443
' | python3 -c 'import sys; print(len({frozenset(l.split()) for l in sys.stdin}))'

blocks.name: slice()
blocks.sum: Build a reusable slice object.

how.text: `seq[a:b:c]` is shorthand for `seq[slice(a, b, c)]`. Name a slice when you cut many records at the same positions, such as fixed-width columns.

examples.desc: Example
examples.code:
line = '10.0.0.1  GET  200'
ip, verb = slice(0, 8), slice(10, 13)
print(line[ip], line[verb], slice(1, 10, 2).indices(5))

examples.desc: Cut the same columns out of every piped line
examples.code: printf '10.0.0.1  GET  200\n10.0.0.9  GET  404\n' | python3 -c 'import sys; ip = slice(0, 8); print([l[ip] for l in sys.stdin])'

blocks.text: Comprehensions
A **comprehension** builds a container from a loop and an optional filter in one expression. It reads like the English sentence "for each x in source, if condition, keep f(x)".

blocks.code:
ports = [22, 80, 443, 8080, 3389, 53]
well_known = [p for p in ports if p < 1024]                  # filter
doubled = [p * 2 for p in ports]                              # transform
labels = ["high" if p >= 1024 else "low" for p in ports]      # transform with an expression
print(well_known, doubled[:3], labels)

lengths = {name: len(name) for name in ["gw", "nas", "router"]}        # dict comprehension
print(lengths)
print({p % 10 for p in ports})                                          # set comprehension

matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
flat = [n for row in matrix for n in row]                     # nested: outer loop first
print(flat)
transposed = [[row[i] for row in matrix] for i in range(3)]
print(transposed)

total = sum(p for p in ports if p > 1000)                     # generator expression: no brackets
print(total)

tokens.exp: the expression: what each kept item becomes
optional filter: only items where this is true are kept

blocks.text: Rules of thumb:

items.text: The expression comes first, then `for`, then `if`. In a nested comprehension the `for` clauses appear in the **same order** as the equivalent nested loops.

Round brackets without a list, `(x for x in ...)`, make a **generator expression**: it produces items one at a time and stores nothing. Pass it straight to `sum`, `max`, `any`, `all` or `join`. That is how you process a log far bigger than memory.
Comprehensions have their own scope, so the loop variable does not leak into the surrounding code.
If it needs more than one filter and one transform, or has side effects, write a normal loop. Readability beats cleverness.

blocks.code:
lines = ["200 /", "404 /missing", "200 /about", "500 /api", "404 /old"]
errors = [ln for ln in lines if ln.startswith(("4", "5"))]
paths = {ln.split()[1] for ln in lines}
gen = (len(ln) for ln in lines)
print(errors)
print(sorted(paths))
print(type(gen).__name__)  # a generator object, nothing computed yet
print(sum(gen), sum(gen))  # exhausted after the first pass

blocks.text: After `sum(gen)` has consumed it, the second `sum` sees nothing and returns 0. If you need two passes, build a list, or recreate the generator.
Sorting

`sorted(iterable)` returns a new sorted list and `list.sort()` sorts in place. Both take two keyword arguments: `reverse=True` for descending, and `key=`, a function applied to each item to produce the value to compare.

blocks.code:
words = ["router", "nas", "Pi", "gateway", "dns"]
print(sorted(words))                       # uppercase sorts before lowercase
print(sorted(words, key=str.lower))        # case-insensitive
print(sorted(words, key=len))              # by length; ties keep original order (stable)
print(sorted(words, key=len, reverse=True))

records = [("gw", 2.4), ("nas", 0.9), ("pi", 12.7), ("tv", 0.9)]
print(sorted(records, key=lambda r: r[1]))                   # by the second field
print(sorted(records, key=lambda r: (-r[1], r[0])))          # latency descending, name ascending

ips = ["10.0.0.10", "10.0.0.9", "10.0.0.100", "10.0.0.2"]
print(sorted(ips))                                           # text order, wrong for addresses
print(sorted(ips, key=lambda ip: tuple(int(o) for o in ip.split("."))))

blocks.text: Three ideas to keep:

items.text: **`key` is called once per item**, and the results are what get compared. The items themselves are returned unchanged.
**Tuples compare element by element**, so a key like `(-count, name)` means "highest count first, then alphabetical". Negating a number reverses just that field.
**The sort is stable**: items with equal keys keep their original relative order. That lets you sort twice, secondary key first, and get a correct multi-level sort.

blocks.code:
from operator import itemgetter, attrgetter
rows = [{"host": "b", "ms": 5}, {"host": "a", "ms": 5}, {"host": "c", "ms": 1}]
rows.sort(key=itemgetter("host"))          # secondary key first
rows.sort(key=itemgetter("ms"))            # then primary key; stability preserves host order
print([r["host"] for r in rows])
print(sorted([3, 1, 2], reverse=True), sorted("hello"), sorted({"b": 1, "a": 2}))

blocks.text: `operator.itemgetter` and `attrgetter` are faster, tidier alternatives to a lambda when the key is just a field. Sorting mixed types, such as `[1, "a"]`, raises `TypeError`.
The collections module
`collections` adds specialized containers to the built-ins. Four of them come up in almost every data script.
Counter: frequency tables

blocks.name: Counter
blocks.sum: A dict subclass that counts hashable items.

how.text: Pass any iterable and each distinct item becomes a key whose value is how many times it appeared. Missing keys count as 0 without raising an error. `most_common(n)` returns the `n` highest pairs, sorted. Counters support arithmetic: `a + b` adds counts, `a - b` subtracts and drops results at or below zero, and `a & b` / `a | b` take the min and max.

examples.desc: Count requests per IP
examples.code:
from collections import Counter
hits = Counter(["10.0.0.5", "10.0.0.9", "10.0.0.5", "10.0.0.5", "10.0.0.9", "10.0.0.2"])
print(hits.most_common(2), hits["10.0.0.99"], sum(hits.values()))
hits.update(["10.0.0.2", "10.0.0.2"])
print(hits["10.0.0.2"], hits + Counter({"10.0.0.5": 10}))

examples.desc: Same answer as `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3`, from the shell
examples.code: awk '{print $1}' access.log | python3 -c 'import sys; from collections import Counter; print(*Counter(sys.stdin.read().split()).most_common(3), sep="\n")'

gotchas: `most_common()` with ties returns equal counts in first-seen order, which is stable but not alphabetical.

blocks.text: defaultdict: grouping without ceremony

blocks.name: defaultdict
blocks.sum: A dict that creates a default value for a missing key on first access.

how.text: The factory is a zero-argument callable (`list`, `int`, `set`, or a lambda). When you read a missing key, the dict calls the factory, stores the result under that key and returns it. `defaultdict(list)` groups items; `defaultdict(int)` totals numbers; `defaultdict(set)` collects unique items per key.

examples.desc: Group ports per host and total bytes per IP
examples.code:
from collections import defaultdict
ports = defaultdict(list)
for host, port in [("gw", 53), ("nas", 22), ("gw", 80)]:
    ports[host].append(port)
size = defaultdict(int)
for ip, n in [("a", 500), ("b", 20), ("a", 700)]:
    size[ip] += n
print(dict(ports), dict(size))

examples.desc: Total bytes per client IP from the log
examples.code: awk '{print $1, $10}' access.log | python3 -c 'import sys; from collections import defaultdict; g = defaultdict(list); [g[ip].append(int(n)) for ip, n in (l.split() for l in sys.stdin)]; print({k: sum(v) for k, v in g.items()})'

gotchas: Merely reading `d[key]` inserts the key. Use `key in d` or `d.get(key)` to test without creating entries.

blocks.text: deque: a queue that is fast at both ends

blocks.name: deque
blocks.sum: A double-ended queue with constant-time appends and pops at both ends.

how.text: A list is slow to pop from the front, because every item shifts. A `deque` is built for it: `append`, `appendleft`, `pop` and `popleft` are all constant time. With `maxlen=n` it becomes a sliding window that silently discards the oldest item when full, a perfect fit for "the last 10 ping times" or "the last 100 log lines".

examples.desc: Keep a moving window of the last 3 round-trip times
examples.code:
from collections import deque
window = deque(maxlen=3)
for ms in [11.8, 12.3, 14.9, 13.0, 12.1]:
    window.append(ms)
print(list(window), round(sum(window) / len(window), 2))
q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.appendleft(0)
print(q.popleft(), q.pop(), q)

examples.desc: Last three lines of a stream, like tail -3
examples.code: seq 1 10 | python3 -c 'import sys; from collections import deque; print(list(deque(sys.stdin.read().split(), maxlen=3)))'

gotchas: Indexing into the middle of a deque is slow. Use it for ends, not for random access.

blocks.text: namedtuple: records with field names

blocks.name: namedtuple
blocks.sum: Create a tuple subclass whose fields can be read by name.

how.text: A named tuple is a real tuple (immutable, unpackable, hashable) with attribute access added, so `rec.ip` replaces `rec[0]`. It uses no more memory than a tuple. Use it for small fixed records that you create in bulk, such as one parsed log line. `_asdict()` converts to a dict and `_replace(field=value)` returns a modified copy.

examples.desc: A parsed log record
examples.code:
from collections import namedtuple
Hit = namedtuple("Hit", ["ip", "status", "size"])
h = Hit("10.0.0.5", 404, 782)
ip, status, size = h
print(h.ip, h[1], h._asdict(), h._replace(status=200))

examples.desc: Parse log fields into named records and read one by name
examples.code: awk '{print $1, $9, $10}' access.log | python3 -c 'import sys; from collections import namedtuple; Hit = namedtuple("Hit", "ip status size"); print([Hit(*l.split()).status for l in sys.stdin])'

blocks.text: OrderedDict and ChainMap

`OrderedDict` was needed before Python 3.7 to remember insertion order. A plain `dict` now does, so you will mostly meet it in older code; its remaining use is `move_to_end()` for building a least-recently-used cache. `ChainMap` links several dicts into one lookup that searches them in order, which models "command-line options override environment variables override defaults" without copying anything.

blocks.name: ChainMap
blocks.sum: Present several dicts as a single mapping, searching them in order.

how.text: A lookup tries the first dict, then the next, and so on. Writes go to the first dict only. Nothing is merged or copied, so later changes in the underlying dicts are visible through the chain.

examples.desc: Layered settings
Layer a setting piped in over the defaults
examples.code: echo timeout=10 | python3 -c 'import sys; from collections import ChainMap; env = dict(kv.split("=") for kv in sys.stdin.read().split()); print(dict(ChainMap(env, {"port": "22", "timeout": "5"})))'

blocks.code:
from collections import OrderedDict
cache = OrderedDict()
for key in ["a", "b", "c"]:
    cache[key] = key.upper()
cache.move_to_end("a")
print(list(cache), cache.popitem(last=False))

blocks.text: itertools: iterator building blocks
`itertools` provides fast, memory-light tools that return **iterators**, objects that hand out items one at a time. Wrap the result in `list()` to see it. These are the ones worth knowing.

blocks.name: itertools.chain
blocks.sum: Iterate over several iterables as if they were one.

how.text: Yields every item of the first iterable, then the second, and so on, without building a combined list. `chain.from_iterable` flattens one level of nesting.

examples.desc: Walk two hosts' ports, then flatten
examples.code:
from itertools import chain
print(list(chain([22, 80], (443,), "ab")))
print(list(chain.from_iterable([[1, 2], [3], []])))

examples.desc: Join piped hostnames with an extra one
examples.code: printf 'gw\nnas\n' | python3 -c 'import sys; from itertools import chain; print(list(chain(sys.stdin.read().split(), ["pi"])))'

blocks.name: itertools.product
blocks.sum: Cartesian product: every combination of one item from each iterable.

how.text: Equivalent to nested `for` loops, as a single iterator. `repeat=n` multiplies an iterable with itself. It is the compact way to enumerate host and port pairs for a scan plan.

examples.desc: Every host and port combination
examples.code:
from itertools import product
plan = list(product(["10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2"], [22, 80]))
print(plan, len(list(product("01", repeat=3))))

examples.desc: Turn piped hosts and two ports into a scan plan and count it
examples.code: printf '10.0.0.1\n10.0.0.2\n' | python3 -c 'import sys; from itertools import product; [print(h + ":" + str(p)) for h, p in product(sys.stdin.read().split(), (22, 80))]' | wc -l

blocks.name: itertools.permutations
blocks.sum: Every ordering of r items from an iterable.

how.text: Yields tuples in which order matters (`ab` and `ba` are different) and no item repeats by position. The count grows factorially, so keep inputs small. `itertools.combinations(it, r)` is the order-insensitive sibling.

examples.desc: Orderings and pairs
examples.code:
from itertools import permutations, combinations
print(list(permutations("abc", 2)))
print(list(combinations(["gw", "nas", "pi"], 2)))

examples.desc: Count the orderings of three piped hosts
examples.code:
printf 'gw
nas
pi
' | python3 -c 'import sys; from itertools import permutations; print(len(list(permutations(sys.stdin.read().split()))))'

blocks.name: itertools.groupby
blocks.sum: Group consecutive items that share a key.

how.text: Yields `(key, group_iterator)` for each **run** of adjacent items with the same key. Like `uniq`, it only sees neighbours, so sort by the same key first or you will get several groups for one key. Consume each group before moving to the next.

examples.desc: Group sorted log lines by status
examples.code:
from itertools import groupby
rows = [("200", "/"), ("404", "/x"), ("200", "/a"), ("404", "/y")]
for status, grp in groupby(sorted(rows), key=lambda r: r[0]):
    print(status, [path for _, path in grp])

examples.desc: Count status codes the way uniq -c does, after sort
examples.code: awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | python3 -c 'import sys; from itertools import groupby; print([(k, len(list(g))) for k, g in groupby(sys.stdin.read().split())])'

gotchas: Without the `sorted`, `200` would appear twice in the output.

blocks.name: itertools.islice
blocks.sum: Slice any iterator, including infinite ones.
blocks.syntax: itertools.islice(iterable, stop)  /  islice(iterable, start, stop, step)

how.text: Iterators cannot be sliced with `[a:b]`. `islice` walks through the unwanted items and yields only the wanted ones, so it works on generators and file objects. Negative values are not allowed.

examples.desc: First three lines of a generator
examples.code:
from itertools import islice, count
squares = (n * n for n in count(1))
print(list(islice(squares, 3)), list(islice("abcdef", 1, 5, 2)))

examples.desc: First three lines of a stream, like head -3
examples.code: seq 1 100 | python3 -c 'import sys; from itertools import islice; print([l.strip() for l in islice(sys.stdin, 3)])'

blocks.name: itertools.accumulate
blocks.sum: Yield running totals (or any running combination) of an iterable.

how.text: By default it adds, so `[1, 2, 3]` becomes `1, 3, 6`. Pass `max` for a running maximum. Handy for cumulative byte counts or detecting when a total crosses a threshold.

examples.desc: Cumulative bytes and running maximum
examples.code:
from itertools import accumulate
sizes = [500, 1500, 200, 800]
print(list(accumulate(sizes)), list(accumulate(sizes, max)))

examples.desc: Running total of response sizes from the log
examples.code: awk '{print $10}' access.log | python3 -c 'import sys; from itertools import accumulate; print(list(accumulate(map(int, sys.stdin.read().split()))))'

blocks.text: Two more tools in `itertools` are `count(start, step)`, an infinite counter, and `cycle(iterable)`, which repeats an iterable forever. Both only make sense with `islice`, `zip` or a `break`:

blocks.code:
from itertools import count, cycle, islice
print(list(zip(count(1), "abc")), list(islice(cycle(["a", "b"]), 5)))

blocks.text: heapq and bisect

Two standard-library modules treat a plain list as something smarter. `heapq` keeps a list arranged as a **heap**, so the smallest item is always first: `heapq.nlargest(3, items)` and `nsmallest` return the top few without sorting everything. `bisect` assumes a list is already sorted and finds an insertion point by binary search, in about 20 steps for a million items.

blocks.code:
import heapq, bisect
latencies = {"gw": 2.4, "nas": 0.9, "pi": 12.7, "tv": 31.0, "ap": 5.5}
print(heapq.nlargest(2, latencies, key=latencies.get))
print(heapq.nsmallest(2, latencies.values()))
thresholds = [100, 500, 1000]                      # sorted
print(bisect.bisect(thresholds, 750), bisect.bisect_left(thresholds, 500))
data = [1, 3, 5]
bisect.insort(data, 4)
print(data)

blocks.text: dataclasses: a first look

When a record needs behaviour, defaults or type hints, a `dataclass` is a tidier alternative to a dict or tuple. You write the fields once and Python generates `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__`. [Classes and objects](#py-oop) covers the details; this is the minimum to recognize.

blocks.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Host:
    name: str
    ip: str
    ports: list = field(default_factory=list)

h = Host("gw", "192.168.1.1")
h.ports.append(53)
print(h, h == Host("gw", "192.168.1.1", [53]))

blocks.text: JSON-shaped data

Nearly every API and config file you will meet is JSON, and JSON maps directly onto what you just learned: objects become dicts, arrays become lists, strings, numbers, `true`/`false`/`null` become `str`, `int`/`float`, `True`/`False`/`None`. The `json` module converts text to these structures and back ([Files and text](#py-files) covers files). Walking a nested structure is just chained subscripts and loops.

blocks.code:
import json
text = '{"site": "home", "hosts": [{"name": "gw", "ports": [53, 80]}, {"name": "nas", "ports": [22, 445]}]}'
data = json.loads(text)
print(data["hosts"][1]["name"], [h["name"] for h in data["hosts"] if 22 in h["ports"]])
data["hosts"].append({"name": "pi", "ports": []})
print(json.dumps(data["hosts"][-1]), len(data["hosts"]))

blocks.text: Network tasks, end to end
Four patterns that cover most day-to-day scripting. Each starts from text, because text is what commands print.
Parse command output into records

`ps aux` prints one process per line with fixed leading columns and a command that may contain spaces. `split(None, maxsplit)` splits on runs of whitespace a limited number of times, keeping the tail intact.

blocks.code:
ps_text = """alice 412 0.3 1.2 /usr/sbin/sshd -D
root 1 0.0 0.1 /sbin/launchd
bob 977 12.5 8.4 /Applications/Safari.app/Contents/MacOS/Safari --new-window
bob 1010 31.0 2.2 python3 scan.py --ports 1-1024"""

procs = []
for line in ps_text.splitlines():
    user, pid, cpu, mem, command = line.split(None, 4)
    procs.append({"user": user, "pid": int(pid), "cpu": float(cpu), "mem": float(mem), "cmd": command})

top = sorted(procs, key=lambda p: p["cpu"], reverse=True)[:2]
print([(p["pid"], p["cpu"]) for p in top])
by_user = {}
for p in procs:
    by_user[p["user"]] = by_user.get(p["user"], 0) + p["mem"]
print(by_user)

blocks.text: Practice

task.text: Write `unique(items)` that returns a list of the distinct items of any list, keeping the order in which each item first appeared.

why.text: Dict keys are unique and keep insertion order, so `dict.fromkeys` removes duplicates while remembering the first occurrence. `list(set(items))` would lose the order. A loop with a `seen` set works too and is easier to extend (for example to unhashable items).

blocks.title: Top talkers

task.text: Write `top_n(items, n)` that returns the `n` most frequent items as a list of `(item, count)` tuples, highest count first. Break ties alphabetically by item.

blocks.solution:
from collections import Counter

def top_n(items, n):
    counts = Counter(items)
    return sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:n]

why.text: `Counter.most_common` breaks ties by first appearance, not alphabetically, so sorting the items yourself with the key `(-count, item)` gives a fully defined order. This is the same as `sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr -k2` in the shell.

blocks.check:
ips = ["b", "a", "c", "a", "b", "a", "d", "c"]
assert top_n(ips, 2) == [("a", 3), ("b", 2)], top_n(ips, 2)
assert top_n(ips, 3) == [("a", 3), ("b", 2), ("c", 2)], "ties should be alphabetical: " + str(top_n(ips, 3))
assert top_n([], 5) == []
assert top_n(["x"], 5) == [("x", 1)]

task.text: Write `group_ports(pairs)` that takes a list of `(host, port)` tuples and returns a dict mapping each host to a sorted list of its distinct ports.

why.text: A `defaultdict(set)` creates the set on first use and drops duplicates for free; a dict comprehension then turns each set into a sorted list. Returning a plain `dict` keeps the defaultdict's insert-on-read behaviour from leaking to callers.

blocks.title: What changed?

task.text: Write `diff_inventory(old, new)` for two dicts that map IP to hostname. Return a tuple `(added, removed, changed)`: `added` is the sorted list of IPs only in `new`, `removed` the sorted list of IPs only in `old`, and `changed` a dict mapping IPs in both whose name differs to the pair `(old_name, new_name)`.

why.text: Dict key views behave like sets, so `-` and `&` give the new, gone and shared addresses directly. The comprehension then compares values only for the shared keys.

blocks.title: Parse ps lines

task.text: Write `parse_ps(text)` that turns lines of the form `user pid cpu mem command...` (the command may contain spaces) into a list of dicts with keys `user`, `pid` (int), `cpu` (float), `mem` (float) and `cmd`. Skip blank lines.

why.text: `split(None, 4)` splits on whitespace at most four times, so the fifth piece keeps its internal spaces. Converting `pid`, `cpu` and `mem` at parse time means the rest of the program works with numbers, not strings.

blocks.title: Break the grid, then fix it

task.text: This function is meant to return a `rows` by `cols` grid of zeros whose rows are independent, but writing to one cell changes a whole column. Fix `make_grid` so that `g = make_grid(2, 3); g[0][0] = 1` leaves `g[1][0]` equal to 0.

blocks.solution:
def make_grid(rows, cols):
    return [[0] * cols for _ in range(rows)]

why.text: The multiplication `* rows` repeats a reference to one row object, so all rows are the same list. The comprehension evaluates `[0] * cols` once per row and builds distinct lists. The same mistake appears as `[[]] * n`, `dict.fromkeys(keys, [])` and mutable default arguments.

blocks.starter:
def make_grid(rows, cols):
    return [[0] * cols] * rows
blocks.check:
g = make_grid(2, 3)
g[0][0] = 1
assert g == [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]], "rows must be independent, got " + str(g)
assert make_grid(0, 5) == []
assert len(make_grid(3, 2)[2]) == 2

questions.q: Which statement about `b = a` where `a` is a list is true?

options.text: It copies the list, so changing `b` leaves `a` alone
It makes a second name for the same list, so changes through `b` show in `a`
It copies only the first level of the list
It raises an error if `a` has nested lists

questions.why: Assignment binds a name to an existing object and never copies. Use `a.copy()`, `list(a)` or `copy.deepcopy(a)`.
`list.sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`. Use `sorted(lst)` when you want the new list.
`get` returns the default when the key is missing and does not insert it.

questions.q: Which of these can be a dict key?
questions.why: Keys must be hashable. A tuple of hashable items is; lists, sets and dicts are mutable and therefore not.

questions.q: Which expression gives the IPs that are in `today` but not in `yesterday` (both sets)?
questions.why: The difference `today - yesterday` keeps elements of the left set that are absent from the right.

questions.q: `sorted(records, key=lambda r: (-r[1], r[0]))` orders the records how?

options.text: Descending by field 1, ties broken by field 0 ascending

questions.why: Tuples compare element by element. Negating the number reverses that field only, and the second element breaks ties.

blocks.text: Project: loganalyzer core

`loganalyzer.py` reads a web-server log and reports who is asking for what. Your Mac's `access.log` in `~/lab` uses the **combined log format**: `ip - - [time tz] "METHOD path proto" status bytes "-" "agent"`. In this chapter you build the core, tested on a small sample string that runs in the page. In [Files and text](#py-files) the same functions gain real files, regular expressions and a command-line interface.
Step 1: Parse a line, then the whole log

The request is inside the first pair of double quotes, status and size follow the second quote. `split('"')` cuts the line on the quote characters, which isolates those parts without a regular expression.

blocks.code:
SAMPLE = '''45.33.32.156 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000] "GET /api/v1/orders HTTP/1.1" 404 782 "-" "curl/8.4.0"
198.51.100.8 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:15 +0000] "GET /images/logo.png HTTP/1.1" 304 0 "-" "Googlebot/2.1"
172.16.5.9 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:42 +0000] "GET /.env HTTP/1.1" 401 365 "-" "Mozilla/5.0"
198.51.100.23 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:15:22 +0000] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 7625 "-" "Mozilla/5.0"
198.51.100.8 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:15:40 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 5120 "-" "Googlebot/2.1"
45.33.32.156 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:16:02 +0000] "POST /login HTTP/1.1" 401 210 "-" "curl/8.4.0"
45.33.32.156 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:16:09 +0000] "GET /admin HTTP/1.1" 404 512 "-" "curl/8.4.0"
198.51.100.23 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:16:30 +0000] "GET /about.html HTTP/1.1" 200 3300 "-" "Mozilla/5.0"
this line is damaged'''

def parse_line(line):
    """Return a dict for one log line, or None if the line is not valid."""
    parts = line.split('"')
    if len(parts) < 3:
        return None
    request = parts[1].split()
    tail = parts[2].split()
    if len(request) != 3 or len(tail) != 2 or not tail[0].isdigit():
        return None
    ip = line.split()[0]
    stamp = line.partition("[")[2].partition("]")[0]
    return {
        "ip": ip,
        "time": stamp,
        "method": request[0],
        "path": request[1],
        "status": int(tail[0]),
        "bytes": 0 if tail[1] == "-" else int(tail[1]),
    }

def parse_log(text):
    """Parse many lines; return (records, number_of_unparsable_lines)."""
    records, bad = [], 0
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if not line.strip():
            continue
        rec = parse_line(line)
        if rec is None:
            bad += 1
        else:
            records.append(rec)
    return records, bad

print(parse_line(SAMPLE.splitlines()[0]))
print(parse_line("this line is damaged"))
records, bad = parse_log(SAMPLE)
print(len(records), "records,", bad, "unparsable")
print(records[3]["ip"], records[3]["status"])

blocks.text: `parse_log` loops over the lines, skips blanks and counts the damaged ones, so a single bad line never stops the run.
Returning `None` for a bad line, instead of raising an error, lets the caller count and skip damaged lines. [Errors and debugging](#py-errors) shows the exception-based alternative.

A new outer container whose items are the same objects as the original's
A copy in which nested containers are copied too, sharing nothing mutable with the original

An expression that builds a list, dict, set or generator from a loop and an optional filter
A comprehension in round brackets that yields items lazily and can be consumed once
A sort that keeps equal items in their original relative order
